simple: a computer system whose answer is only correct if it also arrives on time.
analogy: a drummer who must hit every beat; late is wrong, even if the note is right.
precise: a system whose correctness depends on the logical result and on the time at which it is produced; timing requirements are stated as deadlines on tasks or on end-to-end chains. "Real-time" is not a speed: a slow system can be real-time if it is always on time.
related: Start latency (release jitter at the start)

simple: one run of a repeating task, and the moment it becomes due.
analogy: one beat of the song, and the moment it should sound.
precise: a periodic task with period T releases a job at rk = φ + k·T (φ is the phase, the first release); the job may start at or after its release, never before.
related: Start latency (release jitter at the start)

term: Start latency (release jitter at the start)
simple: how late a job actually began after it became due.
analogy: how long after the beat Amara's stick touched the drum.
precise: sk − rk, where sk is the start time. On an operating system it includes the timer's own lateness, the wake-up and the time until the scheduler lets the task run; F9-48 calls the first part wake-up latency.

simple: how much time a job is allowed, and the clock time by which it must be done.
analogy: "within this beat", and "before the next beat at 3:00:01.250".
precise: the relative deadline D is a property of the task; the absolute deadline of job k is dk = rk + D. D = T is called an implicit deadline, D < T a constrained deadline.
related: Start latency (release jitter at the start)

simple: how uneven the timing is from one job to the next.
analogy: beats that are not evenly spaced.
precise: the variation of a timing quantity over the jobs of a task. It must always be said which quantity: start (release) jitter = max − min of start latency; response jitter = max − min of response time; period jitter = the spread of start-to-start intervals around T. Some texts use the absolute spread, others the largest deviation from the ideal; reports must state the definition.
related: Start latency (release jitter at the start)

simple: how bad it is to be late.
analogy: a missed beat that stops the show, one that is skipped, or one that makes the song a little worse.
precise: a deadline is hard if a miss can cause a failure with serious consequences, firm if a late result is useless but a miss is not catastrophic (the result is dropped), soft if a late result still has some, decreasing, value. The classification belongs to the requirement, not to the code.
related: Start latency (release jitter at the start)

simple: a loop that slowly falls behind its intended schedule.
analogy: a drummer who waits one beat-length after each hit instead of following the conductor: the band slowly gets ahead of her.
precise: the growing difference between the k-th actual release and φ + k·T, caused by computing each release from the previous wake-up (relative sleep) instead of from the fixed schedule (absolute sleep).
related: Start latency (release jitter at the start)

simple: a calculation that says, before running, whether every deadline will be met.
analogy: checking on paper that both drum patterns fit into the bars.
precise: a test on a task set's parameters (T, C, D, and possibly B, J) under a given policy; it is sufficient if "yes" guarantees schedulability, necessary if "no" guarantees a miss, and exact if both.

simple: always run the job whose deadline comes soonest.
analogy: whoever's bar ends sooner plays now.
precise: a dynamic-priority preemptive policy: at every instant the ready job with the earliest absolute deadline runs. On one processor, for independent preemptible jobs, EDF meets all deadlines whenever any algorithm can (it is optimal); for periodic tasks with deadlines equal to periods, the set is EDF-schedulable if and only if U ≤ 1.

simple: a better quick test for rate-monotonic priorities than the classic bound.
analogy: a stricter but fairer check of the band's bar plan.
precise: a set of n periodic tasks with D = T is schedulable under rate-monotonic priorities if Π(Ui + 1) ≤ 2; sufficient, not necessary, and never more pessimistic than the Liu–Layland bound.

simple: time a task waits for a less urgent task that holds something it needs.
analogy: Amara must wait while Jun finishes tightening the drum skin he started on.
precise: in response-time analysis, the longest time a job can be delayed by lower-priority jobs, for example a critical section on a shared lock; with priority inheritance or a priority-ceiling protocol it is bounded by the length of critical sections (F3-40 covered priority inversion).

simple: the most a task's release can be late compared with when it was due.
analogy: the beat that sometimes reaches Amara a little after the conductor's hand moved.
precise: the maximum delay between a job's nominal arrival and its actual release (for example a timer's lateness, F9-45); a higher-priority task with jitter Jj can interfere as if its period were shortened, so RTA uses ⌈(w + Jj)/Tj⌉, and the task's own response time is Ri = wi + Ji.

simple: the most work that must be finished inside any window of a given length.
analogy: how many strokes must fit inside any stretch of counts.
precise: for synchronous periodic tasks, dbf(L) = Σ max(0, ⌊(L − Di)/Ti⌋ + 1)·Ci; EDF meets all deadlines on one processor if and only if dbf(L) ≤ L for every L (the processor-demand criterion), and it is enough to check the absolute deadlines up to a bound such as the hyperperiod plus the largest D.

simple: the time after which the whole pattern of releases repeats.
analogy: the number of counts after which both drummers start a bar together again.
precise: the least common multiple of the periods; for synchronous tasks the schedule repeats every hyperperiod if U ≤ 1.

simple: under overload, one late job makes the next ones late too, in every task.
analogy: one drummer running late pushes everyone after her off the beat.
precise: the behaviour of EDF when U > 1: because priorities follow deadlines, late jobs keep early deadlines and delay jobs of all tasks, so misses spread across the set, whereas fixed priorities confine misses to the lowest-priority tasks.

simple: Linux's EDF policy, where each task books a share of a processor.
analogy: each drummer reserves so many strokes per bar, and the leader refuses a booking that would not fit.
precise: a scheduling policy (value 6 in the installed <linux/sched.h>) set with the sched_setattr system call and a struct sched_attr whose fields include sched_runtime, sched_deadline and sched_period (installed <linux/sched/types.h>); the kernel schedules such tasks by earliest deadline, limits each to its runtime per period, and refuses new reservations that exceed its admission limit.

simple: the rule that says when the kernel may stop what it is doing to run a more urgent task.
analogy: the rider's promise about finishing thoughts.
precise: a build-time (and on some kernels boot-time) choice of how often kernel code checks for and allows rescheduling: never inside the kernel except at explicit points ("none"), at additional voluntary points, almost anywhere outside sections that disable preemption ("full"), or, with PREEMPT_RT, almost anywhere at all. The build container's kernel shows CONFIG_PREEMPT_NONE=y and CONFIG_PREEMPT_DYNAMIC=y.

simple: a way to build Linux so that nearly all kernel work can be interrupted by a more urgent task.
analogy: the rider who drops any thought the moment the bicycle wobbles.
precise: the Linux real-time preemption model: interrupt handlers run in kernel threads, most kernel spinning locks become sleeping locks with priority inheritance, and the remaining non-preemptible regions are kept short, so that the wake-up latency of the highest-priority task is bounded by small, analysable sections. Its configuration option was not present in the build container's kernel configuration.

simple: a stretch of kernel code that nothing else may interrupt to run another task.
analogy: a thought the second rider must finish.
precise: code that runs with preemption disabled (explicitly, while holding a spinning lock, or in interrupt context) or with local interrupts disabled; a task that becomes ready meanwhile cannot run on that processor until the section ends (OS303 introduced the preemption count).

simple: an interrupt handler that runs as a normal kernel task with a priority, instead of immediately.
analogy: a message passed to a helper, who deals with it when the rider's more urgent steering is done.
precise: a handler split into a minimal part in hard-interrupt context, which acknowledges the device and wakes a kernel thread, and the main part, which runs in that thread under a scheduling policy and priority; such threads are named irq/<number>-<name>, and the two on the build container ran as SCHED_FIFO priority 50.

simple: the time from "this task should run now" to "it is running".
analogy: from the wobble to the first steering movement.
precise: for a timer-driven task, the time from the programmed expiry to the moment the task executes its first instruction after the wake-up; it includes timer interrupt latency, the time until the scheduler may run, the scheduling decision and the context switch.

simple: a safety limit that keeps real-time tasks from taking every last moment of a processor.
analogy: the rule that the drummer must leave a short pause each minute for others.
precise: the kernel's limit on processor time for real-time tasks, configured by /proc/sys/kernel/sched_rt_runtime_us per sched_rt_period_us; the build container read 950,000 per 1,000,000 µs (F9-46).

simple: the value below which a given share of the measurements falls.
analogy: the 99th percentile of beats is the lateness that only 1 beat in 100 exceeds.
precise: for n sorted samples, the pth percentile is the sample at a chosen index near p/100·n; Listing 1 uses index ⌊p/100·n⌋, so its "p99.9" of 5,000 samples is the fifth-largest sample. Always state n with a percentile.

simple: a count of how many cycles had each amount of lateness.
analogy: a chart of all the drummer's beats, sorted by how late they were.
precise: counts per lateness bin; for latency the bins are best spaced roughly logarithmically, because the interesting part is the long, sparse tail and not the dense median.

simple: telling the kernel to keep all of the program's memory in RAM and ready.
analogy: laying every stick and brush out before the concert.
precise: mlockall(MCL_CURRENT | MCL_FUTURE) asks the kernel to keep all current mappings and future ones in RAM, so they are not paged out; it does not stop a program from creating new mappings inside its loop.

simple: other work the computer does during the measurement.
analogy: the hot lights and loud audience.
precise: a defined, repeatable set of competing activity (processor, memory, input/output, interrupts) under which the latency is measured; a latency number without its load is not a result.

simple: the chain of code that must finish before the deadline every cycle.
analogy: the drumbeat.
precise: the callbacks and functions between reading the sensor and writing the command in each control cycle, including everything they call; every operation on it must have a bounded, known duration.

simple: a fixed circle of slots where one thread writes and another reads, without waiting for each other.
analogy: a rack of sheet-music pages: the drummer drops each page in; the page-turner takes them out.
precise: a single-producer single-consumer queue of fixed capacity, with head and tail indices updated with atomic release and acquire operations, so neither side ever blocks; when it is full, the producer drops the item and counts it (F2-42).

simple: a loop that never asks for new memory while it runs.
analogy: every stick laid out before the concert.
precise: a code path that performs no heap allocation or deallocation after initialisation (no new, no growing containers, no string building); verified by counting allocations per thread, as Listing 2 does by replacing the global operator new.

simple: the code that connects the control software to one robot's real (or simulated) motors and sensors.
analogy: the nerves between brain and muscles.
precise: in ros2_control, a component that is initialised and activated by the framework, exports named state and command interfaces backed by values it owns, and implements a read step (device → state values) and a write step (command values → device) called every cycle. Listing 2 is a miniature with the same shape.

simple: a named number the controller may read (state) or write (command).
analogy: one nerve fibre, carrying one kind of message.
precise: a pair of a name, conventionally "joint/quantity" such as left_wheel/velocity or left_wheel/effort, and a reference to a value owned by the hardware interface; controllers exchange values through these references, without copying or allocating in the loop.

simple: the piece of code that turns targets and measurements into commands each cycle.
analogy: the brain's steering skill.
precise: a component that declares the interfaces it needs, is configured once with references to them, and implements an update function called every cycle by the controller manager; the update must be real-time safe (no allocation, no blocking, bounded time).

simple: the part that loads controllers, connects them to the hardware, and runs the loop.
analogy: the rhythm of looking, deciding and steering.
precise: the component that owns the hardware interfaces and controllers, assigns interfaces to controllers (refusing a command interface claimed twice), and runs the cycle read → update → write at a configured rate on its own thread.

simple: a written rule for how regular the loop's timing must be.
analogy: "every beat within a tenth of a beat of the click, and never a missed beat".
precise: measurable limits on the loop's period and execution time, with the share of cycles that must meet them and the conditions of the measurement; this chapter's: R1 period within 1,000 ± 100 µs for at least 99.9 % of cycles, R2 no period above 2,000 µs, R3 read + update + write under 200 µs in every cycle.

simple: a version of ROS 2 small enough for a microcontroller.
analogy: the reflex circuit that also reports to the brain.
precise: a framework that runs a reduced ROS 2 client library on a microcontroller with an RTOS, with static memory and a fixed number of entities, and connects to a ROS 2 system through an agent on a larger computer, over a serial, UDP or similar transport (names and details: unverified box in Layer 2).

simple: a program on the big computer that speaks for the microcontroller in the ROS 2 world.
analogy: an interpreter at the border.
precise: a process on the host that receives the microcontroller's compact protocol messages over the transport and creates and operates the corresponding DDS entities (publishers, subscribers) on the client's behalf, so that other ROS 2 nodes see ordinary topics. Listing 2 plays this role for this chapter's own frame format.

simple: a counter put into every message, so that the receiver can see if one is missing.
analogy: page numbers in a book: a missing page is visible at once.
precise: a monotonically increasing number assigned by the producer to each sample when it is produced (not when it is sent), so that losses anywhere between production and reception show as gaps at the receiver.

simple: one packaged message on a stream of bytes, with a start marker, a length and a check value.
analogy: an envelope with the number of pages written on it and a seal.
precise: a delimited unit on a byte stream: a start byte, a length, a payload and a checksum (here CRC-16 with polynomial 0x1021 and initial value 0xFFFF over length and payload), so that the receiver can find message boundaries and reject corrupted messages.

simple: deciding all memory when the program is built, not while it runs.
analogy: a toolbox with a fixed slot for each tool.
precise: every buffer, stack and object has a size fixed at build time and lives in the image's data or zero-initialised (.bss) sections; nothing is allocated at run time, so memory use is known from the linker output (OS305).
